input.reasoning:
Estimation approach: backlog totals 81 story points across 8 tasks. With no historical velocity data for this team, I used an industry-typical planning heuristic of ~6-8 hours of total delivery effort per story point for a mid-complexity web app (covering dev, testing, deployment, and coordination), then allocated that effort across roles based on task nature (backend-heavy items like RBAC, payments, migration; frontend-heavy items like design system, dashboard, invoice UI; QA on all; DevOps on pipeline and migration cutover).

Total estimated effort ~ 81 points x 7 hrs/point avg = ~567 hours of core dev work, then split by role per task and QA/DevOps overlay added, giving the hours below. Role capacity constraints checked against a nominal 6-week (approx 240 working hours per FTE) delivery window:
- Backend Developer: 1.5 FTE => ~360 hrs capacity in window; allocated 350 hrs (fits, tight)
- Frontend Developer: 1.0 FTE => ~240 hrs capacity; allocated 230 hrs (fits, tight)
- QA Engineer: 0.6 FTE => ~144 hrs capacity; allocated 140 hrs (near full capacity - flagged as thin for backlog size)
- DevOps Engineer: 0.4 FTE => ~96 hrs capacity; allocated 90 hrs (thin, concentrated on CI/CD + migration cutover)

Non-labour costs added for Stripe integration sandbox/production fees, Oracle migration tooling/consultancy for schema mapping, and cloud staging environment costs, plus a contingency line for the urgent/high-risk items (payments, migration).

Priority breakdown approximated by allocating each task's estimated total labour cost to its priority tag and summing.

Given RBAC (13pts), Payment integration (13pts) and Legacy migration (21pts) are the largest and highest-risk items, they dominate cost. QA and DevOps are thinly staffed relative to the backlog, which is called out as a schedule/quality risk in assumptions.

No historical actuals were available, so hours are heuristic-based (points-to-hours ratio) rather than derived from past velocity - flagged explicitly as an assumption and a key source of estimate uncertainty, addressed via the scenario percentiles (P50/P70/P90).

scenarios.name: Optimistic / P50 (best-case execution, no major surprises)
Likely / P70 (typical friction, some rework, thin QA/DevOps capacity causes minor delays)
Conservative / P90 (migration complexity, Stripe reconciliation edge cases, RBAC rework)

nonLabourLines.description: Stripe integration setup, sandbox testing and PCI-related review
Cloud staging/CI environment costs (build minutes, hosting) for pipeline setup
Legacy Oracle migration tooling / ETL licenses and DBA consultancy support
Contingency reserve for urgent/high-risk items (payments, migration) - approx 12% of labour

assumptions: No historical actuals (real spend/velocity data) exist for this project; effort was estimated using a heuristic of ~6-8 hours of total delivery effort per story point, adjusted by task type, rather than derived from past performance.

Assumed a nominal ~6-week delivery window; role hours were checked against each role's FTE capacity within that window (Backend 1.5 FTE ~360h, Frontend 1.0 FTE ~240h, QA 0.6 FTE ~144h, DevOps 0.4 FTE ~96h).

QA Engineer (0.6 FTE) and DevOps Engineer (0.4 FTE) are thinly staffed relative to the 81-point backlog; allocated hours are near their capacity ceiling, which is a schedule/quality risk, especially given DevOps also owns the CI pipeline (PW-1) and the legacy migration cutover (PW-8).

Legacy data migration (PW-8, 21 points) assumed to require significant backend engineering plus dedicated non-labour spend for ETL tooling/DBA consultancy due to the scale (400k records, 2M invoice lines) and schema translation from Oracle.

Payment provider integration (PW-7) assumed to require backend + QA + light DevOps effort for webhook infrastructure and reconciliation testing, plus a non-labour allowance for Stripe sandbox/setup costs.

Design system (PW-2) and Invoice list/detail (PW-6) treated as primarily Frontend-Developer-led work with QA support; RBAC (PW-4) treated as roughly even Backend/Frontend split given enforcement is required in both API and UI.
Priority-based cost breakdown is computed by summing each task's estimated labour cost and attributing it to that task's stated priority label.
Contingency of ~12% of labour cost applied given elevated uncertainty (no actuals, complex payment and migration work, thin QA/DevOps capacity).

reductions.description: Descope PW-2 (Design system and component library) to a minimal component set now, deferring full theming tokens and advanced components to a later phase.
reductions.effect: Reduces Frontend Developer hours by ~90 on PW-2; delivers a slimmer but functional component library, with polish deferred.

reductions.description: Reduce QA Engineer scope on Medium-priority items (PW-2, PW-6) to smoke testing only, relying on developer self-testing for full coverage.
reductions.effect: Cuts ~50 QA hours from lower-priority backlog items; increases regression risk on those items, mitigated by keeping full QA on Urgent/High items.

reductions.description: Defer PW-8 legacy data migration's full 2M invoice line migration to a phased rollout (migrate customers + recent invoices first, historical invoice lines later).
reductions.effect: Reduces this phase's Backend Developer and migration-tooling non-labour spend by narrowing initial scope; remaining historical data migrated in a follow-on project phase.

reductions.description: Use a managed Stripe Checkout/hosted integration instead of a fully custom payment UI and reconciliation logic for PW-7's first release.
reductions.effect: Cuts Backend Developer and QA hours on PW-7 by simplifying webhook/reconciliation logic initially, at the cost of some UX customization.

reductions.description: Reduce contingency reserve from 12% to 8% of labour if client accepts higher delivery-date risk given thin QA/DevOps staffing.
reductions.effect: Lowers the non-labour contingency line; increases risk of budget overrun if issues materialize in payments or migration work.
